key_concepts: Momentum depends on mass and velocity
Change in momentum is calculated from starting and ending momentum
Percentage of momentum lost can be computed after impact
Momentum lost in bouncing balls is transferred to sound, heat, or surface deformation
Perfectly elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy
Inelastic collisions do not conserve kinetic energy
In a double-ball drop, a heavier ball can transfer momentum to a lighter ball
An object's mass affects its velocity after collision
Real-life collisions may be partially elastic or inelastic
Conservative collisions retain mechanical energy while non-conservative collisions dissipa
Springs can store and return kinetic energy in elastic-like collisions
Adding clay or holding a spring can make a collision more inelastic
